In London on July 4, 2026, Zendaya appeared at a photocall for *The Odyssey* wearing a pair of gold earrings that have since become the center of a public controversy [Zendaya’s Earrings Are Part of a Much Bigger Problem](https://hyperallergic.com/zendayas-earrings-are-part-of-a-much-bigger-problem/). The objects in question, described as 3,000-year-old discs, were mounted by a jeweler into 18-karat gold and diamond earrings [claim:public-web:3Jj-I5R0Tea9PYw_u0CmtEKvejXC8AqL4QVjmSa61PY:1, 2, 3, 4]. While the jewelry was acquired by the production company, the appearance of these ancient artifacts on a red carpet has triggered critical scrutiny from archaeologists and online commentators [claim:public-web:3Jj-I5R0Tea9PYw_u0CmtEKvejXC8AqL4QVjmSa61PY:4, 7].

## The Provenance of the Hoard

The earrings are reportedly linked to a collection of objects discovered in 1947 near the village of Ziwiye in northwestern Iran [claim:public-web:3Jj-I5R0Tea9PYw_u0CmtEKvejXC8AqL4QVjmSa61PY:18]. This site has long been associated with a famous, though often debated, treasure hoard [claim:public-web:3Jj-I5R0Tea9PYw_u0CmtEKvejXC8AqL4QVjmSa61PY:18]. Many artifacts attributed to this source remain difficult to track, as their movement through the global market has often occurred without clear or documented ownership histories [claim:public-web:3Jj-I5R0Tea9PYw_u0CmtEKvejXC8AqL4QVjmSa61PY:20]. In response to the viral attention, a forensic archive has launched a petition requesting transparency regarding the provenance of the discs [claim:public-web:3Jj-I5R0Tea9PYw_u0CmtEKvejXC8AqL4QVjmSa61PY:9].

## The Mechanics of Repurposing

The process of turning ancient funerary or ritual items into contemporary decorative commodities is a routine practice in the art market, yet it fundamentally alters the status of the objects involved [claim:public-web:3Jj-I5R0Tea9PYw_u0CmtEKvejXC8AqL4QVjmSa61PY:11, 14]. By drilling, cutting, or resetting such artifacts, the original context is physically dismantled, rendering it impossible to preserve or interpret the piece as it was intended [claim:public-web:3Jj-I5R0Tea9PYw_u0CmtEKvejXC8AqL4QVjmSa61PY:16, 17]. This commodification frequently involves reframing ethnographic or archaeological fragments as luxury items, a transformation that standardizes their value while stripping away the history that provided them with meaning [claim:public-web:3Jj-I5R0Tea9PYw_u0CmtEKvejXC8AqL4QVjmSa61PY:11, 14].

## A Wider Cultural Faultline

The controversy underscores a recurring friction between the fashion industry’s appetite for "exotic" ancient motifs and the ethical concerns of the archaeological community [claim:public-web:3Jj-I5R0Tea9PYw_u0CmtEKvejXC8AqL4QVjmSa61PY:6, 8]. Critics have pointed out that the timing of the display is particularly sensitive, given the ongoing destruction of cultural heritage in various regions experiencing conflict [claim:public-web:3Jj-I5R0Tea9PYw_u0CmtEKvejXC8AqL4QVjmSa61PY:10]. As these objects continue to circulate in private collections and global auctions, the debate over whether they belong in museums or as accessories in private hands remains an open question for institutions and collectors alike [claim:public-web:3Jj-I5R0Tea9PYw_u0CmtEKvejXC8AqL4QVjmSa61PY:20]. The incident serves as a visible marker of how the demand for rare materials can inadvertently incentivize the further extraction and dispersal of archaeological finds from their sites of origin [claim:public-web:3Jj-I5R0Tea9PYw_u0CmtEKvejXC8AqL4QVjmSa61PY:19].
